The Least auklet (Aethia pusilla) initiates breeding after a prolonged period of development, with first reproduction occurring at approximately 1095 days from hatching [tR = approximately 1095 days from hatching] under the thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic phase (40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]). This delay reflects the time required to acquire sufficient body reserves in a highly seasonal, pelagic environment where prey availability fluctuates dramatically. The incubation of the single egg lasts approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days] when maintained at a nest cavity temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that is relatively brief for an alcid of this size and likely an adaptation to the short Arctic breeding season. During incubation, the attending parents alternate foraging trips with remarkable coordination, each partner returning to the crevice to relieve the other. The chick that emerges from this egg is well within the expected mass range for the species; neonates weigh approximately 12.3 grams [Wwb = approximately 12.3 grams] at hatching, a modest initial size that nonetheless provides sufficient yolk reserves to sustain the altricial nestling through its first critical hours before parental provisioning begins in earnest.

Fledging marks a significant developmental milestone for the nestling chick, which departs the natal crevice at 29 days after hatching [tx = 29 days after hatching] when the thermal environment is held at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This timing is notably accelerated compared to many other alcid species, an adaptation that minimizes exposure to terrestrial predators such as Arctic foxes and glaucous gulls. The fledgling, once it achieves its first flight, must rapidly develop the foraging skills necessary to capture the abundant copepods that sustain the population. During the post-fledging period, the young bird undergoes a phase of rapid mass gain, eventually attaining the adult body condition typical of the species. The ultimate wet weight measured in fully grown adults is approximately 92 grams [Wwi = approximately 92 grams], though some exceptionally large individuals recorded in field studies have reached as high as 96 grams, reflecting the range of nutritional conditions encountered across different colonies. This adult mass positions the Least auklet as one of the smallest-bodied alcids, a trait that facilitates its aerial agility but constrains its thermal inertia in the cold waters of the Bering Sea.

Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal activity capable of producing viable gametes, is typically reached at 87 days after hatching [tp = 87 days after hatching] under the metabolic conditions of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This rapid sexual maturation is unusual among seabirds and is likely a life-history strategy that compensates for high first-year mortality, allowing individuals that survive the fledgling stage to recruit into the breeding population relatively quickly. The majority of adults, however, do not actually breed until their third year, deferring reproduction in favor of gaining foraging experience and establishing pair bonds. Annual reproductive output is modest but consistent; a typical breeding pair deposits a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and produces exactly one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], resulting in a daily reproduction rate that reflects the constraints imposed by the brief Arctic summer. This low maximum reproduction rate is further shaped by the energetic demands of feeding a rapidly growing nestling on a diet of crustaceans that must be captured during extended foraging bouts.

The maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild is approximately 8.1 years [am = approximately 8.1 years] under the thermal conditions of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], though the vast majority of individuals perish far earlier due to predation, starvation, or storm events during migration. This longevity is comparable to that of other small alcids and reflects a life-history strategy that balances a relatively high potential reproductive output with the substantial risks inherent to foraging in the Bering Sea. Mark-recapture studies from Buldir Island and St. George Island indicate that a small fraction of banded individuals survive past a decade, but the population-level mean is strongly skewed by the high mortality of first-year birds. The energetic costs of reproduction, including egg production and intense chick provisioning, are thought to contribute to the actuarial senescence observed in older breeders, whose body condition declines measurably after several successive breeding attempts. Despite this, some individuals continue to return to the same crevice site year after year, demonstrating a strong fidelity to both mate and nesting location that persists across their entire reproductive life span.

Beyond the core life-history parameters, the foraging ecology of the Least auklet provides additional context for understanding its developmental schedule. During the breeding season, adults may travel up to 80 kilometers from the colony to exploit patches of zooplankton, primarily Neocalanus and Calanus copepods, which are most abundant in surface waters during the brief polar bloom. The chick, once it fledges at 29 days after hatching [tx = 29 days after hatching] under the species' typical body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], must immediately transition from receiving regurgitated meals to independent foraging. This trophic switch is energetically demanding, and field data indicate that fledglings initially lose mass before they develop the proficiency to capture sufficient prey. The energetic demands of these processes are balanced by the remarkably efficient metabolism of this small alcid, which maintains a stable body temperature despite the cold waters it frequents. Comparative studies within the genus Aethia have shown that the Least auklet's combination of early fledging and rapid sexual maturation at 87 days after hatching [tp = 87 days after hatching] at a body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C] is an evolutionary response to intense predation pressure on the colony, favoring a life-history that accelerates development and reduces the duration of terrestrial vulnerability.
